stories.topic: First Brush with FDI: Corning Glass and the Indian State
stories.summary: As a boy in the early 1980s, Ajay was at home when an American visitor from Corning Glass came to meet his father. Corning wanted to build a factory in India to make television picture tubes, and Ajay's father had to explain that the Indian state simply would not allow this — it was banned. The American was utterly baffled: why would a government want to prevent us from building factories in your country? Ajay's father died in 1984, so this scene is fixed in time as a snapshot of License Raj absurdity.
stories.insight: Children of economists absorb economic ideology not from textbooks but from these small, embarrassing scenes — a foreigner offering wealth and being told no. The lifelong love of FDI was kindled by witnessing, up close, the lifelong shame of a country turning it away.

stories.topic: Nokia in Tamil Nadu: The Indian State Eats Its Young
stories.summary: Nokia built a major manufacturing facility in Tamil Nadu — exactly the kind of FDI India claims to want. Then the Indian state went after them with income tax demands and asset freezes. In the end, Nokia simply packed up and left. The state extracted a few rupees and lost the factory, the jobs, and the credibility.
stories.insight: A concrete illustration of why FDI requires not just welcome but a walled-off institutional enclave. Without intellectual clarity about why the foreign firm needs protection from the Indian state's ordinary depredations, even a textbook FDI success story collapses into farce.

stories.topic: From IBM and Coca-Cola to George Fernandez
stories.summary: George Fernandez, as Industries Minister in the late 1970s, drove IBM and Coca-Cola out of India by creating conditions hostile enough that they chose to pack their bags and leave. IBM had been supporting mainframes used by Indian customers; Coca-Cola was a household name. Both vanished overnight on principle.
stories.insight: A reminder that 'shutting down on FDI' isn't an abstraction — it has names, dates, and specific human authors. The same intellectual posture that produced Fernandez's expulsions has reappeared, in less dramatic form, in the Xi Jinping era's technology-transfer mandates and joint-venture rules.

stories.topic: Cafe Coffee Day Is Found in Vienna
stories.summary: While explaining the difference between FDI in India and FDI by India, Ajay drops in that Cafe Coffee Day operates in Vienna, and that he has a photograph to prove it. Indian firms are no longer just receivers of foreign capital — they are themselves becoming multinationals.
stories.insight: The image punctures the old third-worldist self-pity. India is not a passive recipient of FDI exploitation; hundreds of Indian firms are now MNCs with operations across the world. The right frame is graduation, not victimhood.

stories.topic: The Reversal of HMY in Indian Software
stories.summary: The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (HMY) model says the weakest firms stay domestic, better firms export, and the very best do FDI. Ajay and his co-authors found that Indian software companies invert this — the FDI firms are body shoppers, weaker than the pure exporters that sit in India and have foreign business come to them. The highest-productivity Indian software firm is the one that doesn't have to leave home.
stories.insight: A rare empirical anomaly that flips an established model on its head. It also captures something specific about Indian comparative advantage: when your most productive activity is selling brain-power across borders without moving the bodies, the conventional ladder of internationalisation breaks.

core_ideas.concept: FDI as an Institutional Enclave (the Deng Xiaoping Bargain)
core_ideas.explanation: FDI succeeds in poor countries not because foreigners are willing to operate inside bad institutions, but because the state carves out an enclave — typically a small piece of land — where its ordinary depredations don't apply. Inside the enclave: no labour-law harassment, no customs duties, no capital controls, no visa friction, no expropriatory taxation. The ruling elite has to be intellectually honest enough to say openly: our institutions are bad, we won't fix them quickly, so we will build a small island of trustworthy interface for the foreigner. Deng Xiaoping understood this; the Xi Jinping turn (technology-transfer mandates, joint-venture rules) is the loss of that clarity, and FDI into China has duly collapsed.
core_ideas.quote: It is because institutions in China are bad that the great dreamers of China understood — it's gonna take us a hundred years to fix the Companies Act, to fix GST. We're not gonna hold our breath waiting for that. Let's build this enclave.

core_ideas.concept: Knowledge Diffusion Is the Real Gift of FDI
core_ideas.explanation: The deepest case for FDI is not the jobs or the GST receipts. It is that the workers who pass through a foreign firm absorb the global frontier of productivity — how a high-productivity firm actually operates day to day — and then carry that knowledge with them. They leave to work for other firms. They leave to start firms. The crucible is the foreign factory; the diffusion is the entire economy. Bangladesh's garment industry was bootstrapped this way: Taiwanese and Korean firms came in, locals learned the business, the locals then started their own firms.
core_ideas.quote: The ultimate motive force in a society is knowledge. A society only becomes better through the knowledge of its people. We then should view FDI as the crucible where the knowledge is made.

core_ideas.concept: The Seven FDI Numbers (and the Propagandist's Choice)
core_ideas.explanation: There are seven distinct FDI series in the balance of payments: gross FDI inflow into India, gross outflow (repatriation) from FDI in India, net FDI in India; gross FDI outflow by India, gross inflow back, net FDI by India; and net-net (everything combined). Cherry-picking among these seven is how propagandists make India look great or terrible at will. The diagnostic for propaganda: a chart legend that just says 'FDI', without specifying which of the seven it is.
core_ideas.quote: If you say FDI, you are a propagandist. You have to be precise.

core_ideas.concept: FPI Demands Better Institutions Than FDI
core_ideas.explanation: The Indian conventional wisdom — FDI good, FPI bad ('hot money') — is exactly backwards as an institutional matter. FDI can in principle work with a tiny enclave: a three-page rulebook and a state that backs off. FPI cannot. To do portfolio investment you need a hundred years of accounting culture, a stock market, a depository, audit hygiene, the entire institutional apparatus of finance. A Tokyo investor wiring money to buy shares of an Indian company is performing an extraordinary act of institutional faith. India has, by accident of colonial inheritance and reform, more of this institutional richness than China — which is why FPI works in India and not in China.
core_ideas.quote: Contrary to the feelings of many an Indian economist, it is FDI that demands a lower institutional quality, and FPI demands a higher institutional quality.

core_ideas.concept: The Insecurity Hypothesis of FPI Hostility
core_ideas.explanation: The Indian establishment's loathing of foreign portfolio investors as 'hot money' that will 'fly away' is, at root, projection. Foreign investors already know India's institutions are weak — that's priced into the discount they demand on Indian securities. The fear of being abandoned is the fear of an insecure lover. In reality, on any given day there are tens of thousands of foreign buyers and sellers, the net number is small, and there has never been a major crisis caused by foreign portfolio exit from India. The whole 'hot money' narrative is a finance-illiterate story.
core_ideas.quote: If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn't, it never was. That is the right approach to apply to all the great loves of your life, whether FDI or FPI.

core_ideas.concept: The Indian Bourgeoisie's Asymmetric Politics of Foreign Money
core_ideas.explanation: The political economy of FDI vs FPI in India is governed by who benefits in the local elite. FDI is competition: a foreigner building cars in India hurts Premier Padmini's market share. So Indian capital fights it. FPI, by contrast, is pure benefit to incumbent firms — more buyers for their shares lowers their cost of capital. Hence the bizarre Indian inversion in which the harder-to-do thing (FPI) gets a warm welcome and the easier-to-do thing (FDI) gets ideological resistance. The retail anger at Amazon and Walmart is the same logic.
core_ideas.quote: For the Indian rich, FDI is not interesting. FDI is competition for their own businesses. FPI, on the other hand, is very good — I've got a foreigner who will buy my securities.

core_ideas.explanation: Jagdish Bhagwati's coinage for FDI that is not the real thing. If a country erects tariff and non-tariff barriers, foreigners will respond by setting up minimum-effort assembly plants inside the country — bringing in semi-knockdown cars, doing trivial value addition, selling into the protected domestic market. It looks like FDI on paper but is really arbitrage around bad trade policy. Much of the Indian automobile industry was tariff-jumping FDI. The implication: trade liberalisation is a primal requirement; without it, even the FDI you do attract is the wrong kind.
core_ideas.quote: It looks nice. There is some FDI happening into India. But really, what is going on is the trade barriers.

core_ideas.concept: Bilateral Investment Treaties as a State's Self-Slap
core_ideas.explanation: BITs are agreements between India and OECD countries: when the Indian state expropriates a private foreign investor, India agrees to pay them back. It is a brutally honest policy device — the state pre-commits to compensating foreigners for its own future misbehaviour, including misbehaviour by state and city governments. Frontline officials hate paying out, which is exactly why BITs are useful: they deliver a slap that the system would otherwise never receive. The right way to think of the annual BIT payout is as an insurance premium against the loss of FDI confidence: a billion in payouts to stabilise a hundred billion of investment is a bargain.
core_ideas.quote: It is very good to get slapped, because that is the only way you'll create these checks and balances.

core_ideas.concept: FDI Cannot Be a Level Playing Field — and That's the Point
core_ideas.explanation: The instinctive Indian reply to enclave-style FDI is: this is unfair to Indian firms. Ajay's response: yes, accept that. The whole point is that domestic institutions don't work, so the country has to give the foreigner a better deal than it gives its own people, in order to import the productivity and knowledge the country can't yet generate. The complementary task — fighting to extend those same freedoms to Indian firms — is real and ongoing. But refusing to give them to foreigners until Indians have them too is letting the perfect be the enemy of the good.
core_ideas.quote: It is unfair, they are treated better than Indian businessmen. Okay, just accept that, because it is in India's long-term interest to have more global high-productivity firms operating in India.

core_ideas.concept: The HMY Ladder of Firm Internationalisation
core_ideas.explanation: The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model: in any economy, the weakest firms stay purely domestic; medium-productivity firms export; only the very highest-productivity firms do outbound FDI (build operations abroad). It is a ladder of capability. The right diagnostic for the quality of an Indian firm is therefore: are you domestic, exporting, or doing outbound FDI? Hundreds of Indian firms have now climbed onto rung three. Cafe Coffee Day in Vienna is one snapshot of that ladder.
core_ideas.quote: The weakest firms are domestic firms, good firms export, and the highest-productivity firms do FDI. So it's really a journey of graduating.

core_ideas.concept: The Reversal of HMY in Indian Software
core_ideas.explanation: The Indian software industry breaks the HMY model. Pure exporters — companies that sit in India and have foreign business come to them — are the highest-productivity firms. The companies that send bodies abroad ('body shoppers') are the lower-productivity ones doing outbound FDI. The ladder is upside down. The reason has to do with comparative advantage: the most valuable thing Indian software offers globally is its workforce density and cost structure, which is destroyed the moment you ship the bodies abroad.

core_ideas.concept: FDI as a Special Form of Economic Freedom
core_ideas.explanation: Stripped of the jargon, the case for FDI is the case for freedom: the freedom to engage in domestic investment, the freedom to engage with the world, the freedom of the foreigner from the state's predation. The deep anti-foreigner and anti-Western streak in Indian politics is, equivalently, an anti-freedom streak. The cult of third-worldism — that developing countries are helpless victims and multinationals are exploiters — has fed Indian failure for decades, even as the obvious counter-fact has emerged: hundreds of Indian firms have themselves become multinationals.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The framing device: Ajay confides to Amit that he has 'five great loves' in his life — firm productivity, capital account openness, inflation targeting, R programming, and FDI. Amit treats the confession with mock-romantic gravity. 'Oh my god, you almost came as you said that. Continue.'

Amit, on Ajay's intensity about FDI: 'Tell me about the first time you guys met, you and FDI. How did you get acquainted with FDI? Like at first she would have been a stranger, but then she would have you know you would have gotten a little more familiar, then there would have been an attraction. Then there would have been that magic moment where everything clicked.'

Amit, on the seven different FDI series and Ajay's pedantic insistence on legending them: 'You have terrified me. I'm never gonna say FDI in front of you again. Straight away you'll be like — net inflow, gross inflow.'

Ajay's reframe of the FPI insecurity complex as Bollywood romance: 'If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn't, it never was. That is the right approach to apply to all the great loves of your life, whether FDI or FPI.'
Amit on the SEZ vs FDI debate: 'On one side of the debate you have securities, on the other side you have insecurities.'

Amit's libertarian aside: 'When I first heard the concept of SEZs, my purest libertarian mind reacted by saying, why do we need SEZs? A whole country should be an SEZ. Into that heaven of freedom, my father, let my country awake' — Tagore-pastiche applied to the special economic zone.
Amit, on Ajay's faith in the Indian state: 'You expect the Indian state to be humble — like khush ho gaye.' The bureaucrat as reluctant gentleman.

Ajay on the show's growing reach: 'This show, which has a 70% Indian audience and a 30% overseas audience, is an exporting show — because thirty percent of a global audience is coming into this show. You have graduated.' Amit panics in mock-character: 'I am worried apni exporting firm pe income tax laga jayega. My head is spinning, bro. Calm down. We don't know nobody outside India watches.'
Ajay's romantic rebuttal of FDI scarcity thinking: 'The good thing is that FDI is liberal with her affections. We do not have to compete. We can both get FDI.'

Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman — the 1992 Aziz Mirza film, used as the chapter title and metaphor for Indian firms graduating into global firms. 'Raju ko gentleman banna hai. Indian firms want to be global firms.'

George Fernandez expelling IBM and Coca-Cola from India in the late 1970s — invoked as the canonical Indian act of self-harm against FDI and as the template that the Xi Jinping era is now repeating in China.
Vodafone and the retrospective taxation episode (the Madame Mukherji clause) — invoked by Amit as the standing example of how the Indian state destroys the predictability that FDI requires.
Premier Padmini — the Hindustan Motors / Premier Automobiles staple of License-Raj India, used as shorthand for the protected domestic incumbent threatened by foreign carmakers.
The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple (HMY) model — the canonical economic-trade-theory ladder: domestic firms < exporters < FDI firms.
Jagdish Bhagwati's coinage 'tariff-jumping FDI' — invoked from his early-1990s critique of the first wave of FDI into post-1991 India.
Deng Xiaoping vs Xi Jinping — used throughout as a binary: Deng as the patron saint of FDI clarity, Xi as the destroyer of the bargain.
